idiom_name: IEnumerable<T> iterator method using yield return over a local state
implementation_notes: C# absorbs the generator into the language: a method returning IEnumerable<T> that contains yield return is compiled into a state machine producing one element per MoveNext(), so the step function and the scheme collapse into an ordinary while loop plus yield and no combinator is needed. MoreLINQ's Unfold<TState, TResult>(seed, generator) provides the explicit first-class form when the step function must be a value, and the same coalgebra goes push-based as Observable.Generate. Prefer iterators for lazy pull sequences; the classic building blocks are still justified when the step function has to be composed or reused.
pitfalls: The sequence's state must live in locals: a field-based state makes two concurrent enumerations interleave and produces different results per enumeration.
Iterator methods are lazy, so argument validation does not run until the first MoveNext() - guard clauses at the top of the method execute too late.
Breaking out of a foreach leaves the state machine suspended inside try/using blocks; foreach disposes it, but a hand-rolled GetEnumerator() caller must call Dispose.

variants.name: Push-based unfold with Rx Observable.Generate
variants.implementation_notes: Rx.NET supplies the same coalgebra with the consumer inverted: each state is projected to a value and pushed to subscribers until the condition fails, optionally paced by a scheduler, and the subscription's Dispose is the cancellation point. Choose it for event-like or time-based sequences and hot producers rather than for lazy pull enumeration, and remember each subscription replays the unfold.
pitfalls: Without a scheduler the sequence is emitted synchronously on the subscribing thread, so a long unfold blocks the caller.
Generate is cold per subscription: every Subscribe replays the whole unfold, which is wasteful when the step function is expensive.
